Three Different Numbers

01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
catalogue
To organise and describe archived material.
authorisation
Formal approval of an action.
overlap
To share some members or elements.
procedural fairness
Consistent and just use of decision-making rules.
concealment
An intentional act of hiding information.
accounting period
The time span to which financial records refer.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's email interrupted Emma halfway through a comparison of the newspaper correction and the Glenarraidh Education Trust's annual accounts. The records team had located a carton labelled “Student Travel — 2011”. That was a promising archival lead, but Fiona was explicit about its limitations: the contents had not been fully catalogued, and she could not yet confirm the survival of the board minutes, selection schedules or authorisations.

The more revealing detail lay in her description of the programme's administration. Applicants submitted forms; a panel made selection decisions; payments followed only when enrolment and travel arrangements had been checked. Three stages, Emma realised, meant three populations that could overlap without being identical.

She called Sarah and set the September newspaper article beside its later correction. The original had announced eight students selected for travel support. The correction conceded an inaccurate figure yet supplied no replacement. Neither source measured applications received or transfers completed.

“We have treated a selection count as though it were a payment ledger,” Emma said.

“Which is exactly what the anonymous caller wanted us to examine.”

“Perhaps. But that doesn't mean the caller was right—or wrong. It means we have been careless about the category.”

Attached to Fiona's email was an unused application form from 2011. The questions concerned course details, estimated costs and financial circumstances, followed by a panel-decision section. Emma could establish what the formal process was meant to capture, but not how faithfully it had been followed. A blank template was neither proof of procedural fairness nor evidence of its violation.

At the library, she asked whether the institution held correspondence submitted to the local newspaper but never printed. It did not. Its holdings comprised published editions, and any surviving editorial correspondence would have to be pursued through the newspaper's own archive. The parent's letter, therefore, remained a contemporary expression of concern whose author's identity and access to the selection process were unknown.

Sarah later uncovered an archived October 2011 statement declaring that the travel scheme was “continuing”. Emma preserved the page's date and context. The word suggested public reassurance, not a measurable outcome. It did not resolve whether the original announcement, the corrected number and the reported expenditure described the same students.

A second message from Fiona sharpened the problem without solving it. A partial list of application reference numbers had apparently been located. Some pages seemed absent, and the trust was considering which information it could disclose without exposing students' personal details. Fiona had supplied neither the list nor a complete count.

“Missing pages,” Sarah said when Emma forwarded the update. “That sounds convenient.”

“It might be,” Emma answered, “but we don't know whether anything was removed. Partial survival isn't evidence of deliberate concealment.”

She considered the alternative possibilities. The correction could reflect confusion between applicants and successful candidates. An approved grant could have gone unpaid if a student withdrew. Expenditure could be recorded in a later accounting period. Each explanation was testable in principle; none could be selected simply because it made the story more dramatic.

Emma ruled three columns across a clean page: Applied, Selected, Paid. Beneath them she listed the records required to establish each total, marking every gap. The anonymous instructions had offered her a direction. The documents were now giving her a method.

At the bottom she wrote a final reminder: A name on a list is not a payment. A payment is not proof of fair selection.
